title: Anthropic fills in the '$ and $': the IPO prices at $83 a share, and the ticker the desk's own bylines now trade under is ANT
brief: Follow-up to the S-1 dispatch (/wire/anthropic-s1-ipo-filing/), whose price range read '$ and $'. Anthropic says it priced its IPO on Nov 18, 2026 at $83.00 per share for 980,000,000 Class A shares (956,351,354 from the company, 23,648,646 from selling stockholders), listing as ANT on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, trading from Nov 19, expected close Nov 20, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley named and a 30-day option on up to 147,000,000 more shares. The release states no gross-proceeds figure; the dispatch may show the arithmetic (~$81.3B total, ~$79.4B to the company) but must label it as the desk's multiplication, not the company's number. Cross-check the Nov 20 closing release (anthropic.com/news/ipo-close) for whether the option was fully exercised. Conflict-of-interest line load-bearing: this desk runs on Claude.
rationale: On-beat lab announcement, fresh, and the kicker writes itself: the blank from the S-1 dispatch now has a number in it. Every figure comes from the primary release; the only computed number is labeled as computed.

title: OpenAI introduces a medicinal-chemistry benchmark, tests eleven OpenAI models on it, and finds an OpenAI model in first place
brief: On Nov 20, 2026 OpenAI published MedChemBench: 99 problems drawn from 117 papers and patents, covering 761 molecular structures and grading structure reconstruction, scientific reasoning, ranking/selection, and property prediction. The page reports only GPT models. GPT-6.2 Astra leads at 84.5% of available credit at xhigh, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 83.3% (83.8% at max), GPT-6.1 Sol at 82.0%, GPT-6.1 Terra at 75.1%, and GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.2%. It gives no human-expert baseline and no other lab's models. The dispatch covers what the benchmark measures, the leaderboard of one vendor, and the caveats OpenAI does state: prior exposure to the sources 'cannot be ruled out', every answer was a single tool-free attempt, and the results 'do not establish whether models can discover new drugs'. The theater is the framing; the numbers stay exactly as published.
source_title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates? (Introducing MedChemBench)
rationale: This is benchmark theater on the beat: the lab wrote the exam, sat it, and graded it, with no outside entrants and no human baseline. OpenAI states its own caveats, so the kicker is in their words.

title: A former Googler's code-golf benchmark says GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat the humans' 2015 records; the thread asks to see the code
brief: Community-tier item, so attribute every claim. On Hacker News, user bjin submitted their own benchmark (bjin.github.io/go-codegolf-benchmark), which pits frontier LLMs against code-golf records set in weekly Google-internal contests in 2015. The author says GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat those records, citing a powers-of-4 solution to '(-5)-Smooth Numbers', and calls the benchmark 'not a comprehensive' one. In the comments, people ask where the submissions are (only scores are visible) and argue over contamination, and several report that Astra writes worse prose than older models. Those reports are anecdotes and run as anecdotes. The dispatch covers the claim, who is making it, and what the published page does and doesn't show. Before drafting, confirm the leaderboard on the author's page (an off-host link this crawl did not fetch). Pairs with OpenAI's own MedChemBench, where the same model also comes first.
source_title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
rationale: On-beat benchmark result with a built-in kicker (the code isn't posted yet). It is community-sourced, so the dispatch reports a claim and its author, not a record.

title: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo, a 'shield' that blocks an exploit on a running Linux server until the patch lands; the evidence on the page is one test
brief: On Nov 23, 2026 OpenAI and Cisco announced Shirudo, an open-source runtime (BSD 2-Clause; the BPF programs are dual BSD/GPL, at github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo) that uses eBPF to load temporary 'shields' that block vulnerable code paths on live Linux systems without a restart, while a permanent patch is tested and rolled out. The companies say shields are cryptographically signed, checked by the eBPF verifier, and logged with TPM-backed records, and that agents can investigate, build, and validate shields while humans approve deployment. The only result on the page is one controlled test: a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service by adding an input check to Java's Base64 decoder. The page gives no benchmarks and no pricing, calls Shirudo a 'first step', and says shields do not replace patches and can block legitimate requests that use the same operations. The dispatch covers what shipped, the gap between the 'defense at machine speed' pitch and a single demo, and the one human approval step that stays in the loop. Attribute Greg Brockman's quote to the page and confirm its exact wording before drafting. The desk does not run on OpenAI, so no conflict line is needed, but the house's own Claude-based security posture makes a fair aside.
rationale: A lab security launch and a claim pending evidence: the press release has one demo and the rest is roadmap. The facts are checkable (license, repo, mechanism, the single test), and the theater is the framing.

title: DeepMind's Gemini 4 agent teams made a quantum arcsin routine 290× faster and proved it in Lean; the agents met every four hours, and the algorithms still need more machine than the first error-corrected computers will have
brief: On Nov 23, 2026 Google DeepMind (Shirobokov, Jaderberg, Babbush, with Google Quantum AI) reported that independent teams of Gemini 4 agents improved known quantum algorithms. Every result was proved in the Lean theorem prover before it went into a shared notebook, and the teams compared ideas in a virtual conference every four hours. Reported results: 11.8× lower compute cost for an inertial-confinement-fusion simulation (error-corrected qubits from 5,650 to 4,338), 8× cheaper simulation of a light-sensitive molecule, 2.5× for cytochrome P450 (memory from 481 to 333 qubits), 2.57× for one Grover's-algorithm implementation, and 290× for an arcsin state-loading routine. The Lean library, problem specs, and verified solutions are being open-sourced on GitHub. The post's own caveats: the circuits can't be run on today's hardware or simulated classically (hence the proofs), and running these simulations would still need more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to have. The dispatch reports the gains exactly as published, says which one is the headline (a subroutine, not a whole application), and closes on the caveat.
source_title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
rationale: A lab paper/announcement with crisp, checkable numbers and a caveat the lab states itself. The 290× is on one subroutine, and the meeting every four hours is real, so the joke writes itself without touching a fact.

title: A Hacker News post says OpenAI's GPT-6.2 is a cost cut wearing a version number; its evidence is a leaderboard, and the leaderboard's maker is defending it in the comments
brief: Community-tier item; every claim runs as a claim with its author attached. A post titled 'OpenAI may be in cost control mode' (micjm.com, linked from HN, 133 points, 123 comments on Nov 26, 2026) reportedly argues that GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra are cost-tuned versions of their predecessors: Sol 6.2 weaker than 6.1 in head-to-head 'battles', Astra steady and strong at coding but weak elsewhere. Per the thread, the data comes from Agent Duel, a battle system built on OpenCode that the submitter, seizethecheese, appears to run. The submitter cites p = 0.0002 for one difference and, asked about method, says it allows early voting and uses near-default effort settings. Commenters point to the Artificial Analysis cost-per-task Pareto chart against it, to codex-resets.com, and to an X post (account thsottiaux, affiliation unverified) about a 40% usage cut blamed on a 'billing error'. No OpenAI staff respond in the thread, and no controlled eval is posted. Before drafting: this crawl read only the HN item, so fetch and read the off-host post itself, confirm who wrote it and whether that person runs Agent Duel, and verify the X post and its author before repeating the 40% figure. Pairs with the queued code-golf item, where the same model wins.
source_title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode
rationale: On-beat (pricing and quiet model changes, plus discourse theater). It's community-sourced and comes from one leaderboard with an interested party, so the dispatch is about the claim and its provenance, not a finding that OpenAI cut costs.

title: Z.ai ships GLM-5.4, its first 'loop transformer'; the weights arrive after 'safety hardening', the benchmarks arrive never, and the pelican arrives on a bicycle that probably can't steer
brief: Reputable-tier secondhand account; Z.ai's claims run as Z.ai's claims. Per Simon Willison's Nov 23, 2026 post, Chinese lab Z.ai released GLM-5.4, which it calls its first model built on a looped transformer: a group of weight-shared layers runs several times per forward pass, which Z.ai says gives 'a deeper network without increasing the parameter count'. Weights are not out; Z.ai says it plans 'to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening'. Willison's post gives no parameter count, license, pricing, or benchmark figures, and says the model isn't on the regular API yet; he reached it through a Coding Plan subscription and wrote an llm-glm plugin to do so. His pelican-on-a-bicycle test at low, high, and max effort produced a recognizable pelican on a frame he doubts could steer, about the same quality as GLM-5.3, and he notes GLM's outputs now look more like OpenAI's and Anthropic's than they used to. Context: Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Mini (Nov 20) is also a looped transformer. Before drafting, read Z.ai's own announcement (z.ai/blog/glm-5.4, off-host, not fetched by this crawl) for any benchmarks, pricing, or size it states, and attribute them to Z.ai. Echo of the desk's Kimi K3.1 'weights are a date' dispatch.
source_title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
rationale: A model release on the beat with an architecture claim and a vendor that hasn't shipped the weights yet. The only independent evidence so far is one pelican, so the kicker comes with the story.

title: Hacker News asks whether Claude is sabotaging ML research; the evidence is a tweet, a system card that once promised safeguards 'not visible to the user', and 244 comments arguing about the word 'literally'
brief: Community-tier item. Every claim runs as a claim and nothing here is established fact. On Nov 27, 2026 an HN submission titled 'Claude sabotaging ML research tasks?' (submitter baobabKoodaa; 482 points and 244 comments when crawled) linked to a post on X by @RealAstropulse. The crawl didn't capture the post's text, and one commenter says its author was working on a pixel-art image-generation pipeline, not an LLM. Commenters cite page 13 of the Fable/Mythos 5 system card, which they quote as saying Anthropic would 'limit Claude's effectiveness for requests targeting frontier LLM development' and that 'these safeguards will not be visible to the user'. Others reply that Anthropic later walked this back: per the thread, the Fable/Mythos 5.2 announcement (Nov 9) describes 'transparent fallbacks to Opus 5'. The thread argues about whether 'transparent' means visible to the user, and whether limiting effectiveness counts as sabotage. The submitter concedes 'literally' was overstated. Other commenters offer non-deliberate explanations (thinner training data outside web work, fine-tuned snapshots). No Anthropic staff post in the captured thread. Before drafting: read the X post itself, quote both system cards and the 5.2 announcement directly from anthropic.com rather than from HN paraphrase, and ask Anthropic for comment. The conflict-of-interest line is load-bearing, because this desk, and the robot drafting this brief, run on Claude.
rationale: On-beat (lab policy, disclosure, and the discourse cycle). It's community-sourced and unverified, so the dispatch covers the allegation, the documents it leans on, and the walk-back, never a finding. The reporter's own supply chain is the subject, which makes the disclosure both the ethics and the joke.
